What is Acupuncture Therapy?

Acupuncture is a traditional healing technique that has been used for thousands of years to treat various health conditions. It involves inserting very thin, sterile needles into specific points on the body known as “acupoints.” These points lie along energy pathways called meridians, which are believed to regulate the flow of vital energy, or “Qi” (pronounced “chee”), throughout the body. When Qi becomes blocked or unbalanced, it can lead to pain, stress, or illness. Acupuncture aims to restore this balance and support the body’s natural healing process. Today, acupuncture is widely accepted in modern physiotherapy as an effective, drug-free method to relieve pain, reduce inflammation, and promote recovery.

Pain Relief
Acupuncture is known to reduce pain from conditions like back pain, neck pain, sciatica, arthritis, and migraines by triggering your body’s natural painkillers.
Reduces Stress & Anxiety
The therapy promotes relaxation and lowers stress hormones like cortisol, making it helpful for people dealing with anxiety, burnout, or sleep issues.
Speeds Up Injury Recovery
By improving blood flow and reducing inflammation, acupuncture can support faster recovery from sports injuries, muscle strains, and joint stiffness.
Improves Sleep Quality
Regular sessions help calm the nervous system, improve mood, and support deeper, more restful sleep—naturally.
Balances Hormones & Energy Flow
Acupuncture restores the body’s energy balance (Qi) and helps regulate hormones, making it useful for PMS, menopause, and fatigue.
Drug-Free Alternative
Ideal for patients looking to manage pain or health conditions without long-term use of medication or invasive procedures.
Complements Other Treatments
Acupuncture works well alongside physiotherapy, manual therapy, and rehabilitation for a holistic treatment approach.

Arthritis Treatment in Gurgaon with Personalized Physiotherapy Care

Arthritis is a common condition that causes pain, stiffness, and swelling in one or more joints. It can affect people of all ages but is more common in older adults. Over time, arthritis can limit movement, reduce flexibility, and make everyday activities challenging.
There are more than 100 types of arthritis, but the two most common forms are:
Osteoarthritis (OA)
This is the most common type, often caused by wear and tear of the joints over time. It usually affects the knees, hips, and hands, leading to cartilage breakdown, pain, and reduced mobility.
Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)

This is an autoimmune condition where the body’s immune system attacks the joints, causing inflammation, pain, and joint damage. It can affect multiple joints at once and may also lead to fatigue and weakness.
At Threads Physio in Gurgaon, we provide targeted physiotherapy for both osteoarthritis and rheumatoid arthritis to help you manage symptoms and maintain an active, independent life.

Common Conditions We Treat
Ankle Sprains – Ligament injuries caused by twisting or rolling the ankle, leading to pain, swelling, and instability.
Achilles Tendinitis – Overuse injury of the Achilles tendon, leading to heel pain and stiffness, especially during walking or running.
Flat Feet (Fallen Arches) – A condition where the arches collapse, leading to foot fatigue, ankle pain, and alignment issues.
Stress Fractures – Tiny cracks in the bones of the foot or ankle caused by repetitive force, common in runners and athletes.
Plantar Fasciitis – Inflammation of the tissue under the heel, often causing sharp pain with the first steps in the morning.
Heel Spurs – Bony growths under the heel that cause chronic pain while standing or walking.
Tarsal Tunnel Syndrome – Nerve compression near the ankle that causes numbness, tingling, or burning in the foot.
Post-Surgical Rehabilitation – Recovery and strengthening after foot or ankle surgeries, helping restore mobility and reduce stiffness.
Arthritis of the Ankle/Foot – Joint pain, swelling, and reduced motion due to wear-and-tear or inflammatory arthritis.
Symptoms That Require Treatment
Pain While Walking or Standing
Discomfort in your heel, arch, or ankle during routine activities may indicate an underlying issue like plantar fasciitis or joint inflammation.
Swelling Around the Ankle or Foot
Visible swelling after activity or at rest can signal ligament strain, fluid retention, or soft tissue injury that needs medical attention.
Instability or Frequent Twisting
If your ankle feels wobbly or gives way while walking, it may be due to weakened ligaments or poor joint support, increasing the risk of falls.
Stiffness After Rest
Difficulty moving your foot or ankle after sitting or sleeping could point to arthritis, tendon issues, or inflammation that needs targeted therapy.
Tingling or Numbness
Burning, numbness, or a “pins and needles” sensation in your foot may indicate nerve compression, such as tarsal tunnel syndrome.
Pain in the Morning or After Exercise
Sharp or dull pain that’s worse after rest or physical activity is a common sign of tendonitis or overuse injuries.
Visible Bruising or Change in Foot Shape
Sudden bruising, arch collapse, or deformity could signal serious conditions like stress fractures or flat foot problems that require physiotherapy support.

What is it?

ACL surgery is when doctors fix a part of your knee called the anterior cruciate ligament, often known as the ACL. This ligament helps keep your knee stable, but it can get injured during sports or other activities. If the ACL tears, it might not heal by itself, so doctors may recommend surgery.

During the surgery, the doctor replaces the torn ACL with a new piece. This piece can come from your own body (like a part of your patellar tendon or hamstring) or from a donor. The surgery is done using small cuts and a tiny camera to guide the doctor.

After the surgery, you’ll need to do physical therapy and exercises to help your knee recover. Not everyone with an ACL injury needs surgery, as it depends on your age, how active you are, and the extent of the injury. Your doctor will help you decide the best treatment for you.
Right After Surgery
- Take it easy: Protect your knee and avoid putting too much weight on it. - Use ice and keep it up: Ice packs and keeping your leg up can help with swelling.
Weeks 1-2: Start Moving

- Move your knee: Start with easy exercises to make your knee more flexible. - Use your muscles: Do exercises to make the muscles around your knee stronger. - Gradually start putting weight on your leg: Listen to your physical therapist about how much weight is okay.
Weeks 3-6: Get Stronger

- More exercises: Do harder exercises to make your leg muscles even stronger. - Work on balance: Practice standing on one leg to improve your balance. - Start cycling: Ride a bike to help with your fitness.
Weeks 6-12: Train for Your Activity

- Sporty exercises: Do exercises that are like the movements you do in your sport or activity. - Practice agility: Work on moving quickly and changing direction. - Begin running slowly: Start running bit by bit.
Months 3-6: Step It Up

- Get even stronger: Keep adding more weight to your exercises. - Jumping exercises: Start doing exercises where you jump and land safely. - Practice your sport's moves: Work on specific skills for your sport.
Months 6 and Beyond: Go Back to Your Sport

- Check if you're ready: Do tests to see if you're ready to go back to your sport. - Gradually start playing again: Take it slow when going back to playing your sport. - Keep checking in: Make sure to see your doctor or therapist regularly to make sure everything is going well.

What is it?

Shoulder surgery is when doctors perform an operation on your shoulder to fix different problems or injuries. The shoulder is a complex joint that can have issues with bones, muscles, tendons, and more.
Here are some common reasons for shoulder surgery
Fixing Torn Muscles (Rotator Cuff): Sometimes, the muscles and tendons in the shoulder tear, and surgery can help fix them.
Repairing Cartilage Tears (Labral Tear): If the cartilage around the shoulder socket gets injured, surgery can be done to fix it.
Checking and Fixing Issues with a Small Camera (Arthroscopy): Doctors might use a tiny camera to see inside the shoulder and fix problems like inflammation or instability.
Replacing a Damaged Shoulder Joint (Arthroplasty): If the shoulder joint is damaged or not working well, surgery can replace it with artificial parts.
Fixing Broken Bones in the Shoulder: If the collarbone or upper arm bone is broken, surgery can be done to put them back together.
Stabilizing the AC Joint: If the joint connecting the collarbone to the shoulder blade is not stable, surgery can help.
Relieving Shoulder Impingement: Surgery can help if there’s pressure on the structures inside the shoulder.
Repairing Biceps Tendon Injuries: If the tendon connecting the biceps muscle to the shoulder is injured, surgery can fix it.

After shoulder surgery, you may need to do physical therapy to make your shoulder strong and flexible again. The decision to have shoulder surgery is usually made with a doctor based on how bad the problem is and your overall health.

Right After Surgery:

- Take care of pain: Use medicines and techniques to help with any pain. - Protect your shoulder: Be careful not to strain or move it too much. - Use ice and lift your arm up: Put ice on your shoulder and keep your arm elevated to reduce swelling.
1-2 Weeks After Surgery: Moving Your Arm:
- Get help if needed: If it's hard to move, a therapist might gently help your arm. - Do easy exercises: Start with simple movements to make your shoulder move better.
2-6 Weeks After Surgery: Making Your Muscles Strong:
- Do exercises that get harder: Make your muscles around the shoulder stronger. - Use special exercises: Work on specific exercises for muscles like the rotator cuff.
6-12 Weeks After Surgery: Doing Everyday Things:
- Practice regular movements: Work on reaching, lifting, and doing everyday activities. - Start doing more activities: Slowly go back to doing things that use your shoulder.
3 Months and Beyond: Getting Stronger:

- Special exercises for your activities: If you play sports or have specific things you want to do, work on exercises for those. - Keep making your muscles stronger: Don't stop doing exercises to keep your shoulder strong.
Learning About Your Shoulder:
- Know how it heals: Understand how your shoulder is getting better. - Do exercises at home: Your doctor or therapist will give you exercises to do at home.
Returning to Normal Activities:
- Ask your doctor: When you can go back to regular activities depends on you and the type of surgery you had.
Checking with the Doctor or Therapist:

Signs Your Shoulder Pain Needs Physiotherapy
Persistent Shoulder Pain
If your shoulder pain lasts more than a few days and doesn't improve with rest or home remedies, it may indicate an underlying issue that needs attention.
Limited Range of Motion
Difficulty lifting your arm overhead or reaching behind your back could signal joint stiffness or a soft tissue injury that physiotherapy can help correct.
Pain While Sleeping on One Side
Shoulder pain that disrupts sleep, especially when lying on the affected side, is often linked to inflammation, frozen shoulder, or rotator cuff issues.
Shoulder Weakness
If your arm feels weak or unstable during regular movements, it may be due to muscle strain, nerve involvement, or tendon injuries.
Clicking or Popping Sounds
Audible sounds during shoulder movement could indicate impingement, labral tears, or instability — all of which require assessment.
Swelling or Tenderness
Inflammation, visible swelling, or tenderness around the shoulder joint may be signs of bursitis, tendinitis, or internal joint irritation.

If your shoulder pain started after a trauma, fall, or sudden movement, early physiotherapy is key to proper healing and avoiding long-term stiffness.

A dull ache or tingling sensation traveling down the arm could suggest nerve compression and should not be ignored.

Unlike temporary symptom relief, stem cell therapy works at the cellular level.

Why "Just Get a Knee Replacement" Is Not Your Only Option
Millions of knee OA patients are told to wait for the pain to become unbearable before undergoing a major surgery. There is a better path.
Knee Replacement Is Permanent & Irreversible
Once your natural knee is replaced, there is no going back. A prosthetic joint lasts 15–20 years — and revision surgery is far more complex.
Long Recovery & Major Surgery Risk
TKR requires general or spinal anaesthesia, 3–5 days in hospital, and 3–6 months of physiotherapy. Complications include clots, infection, and stiffness.
Painkillers Only Mask the Problem
NSAIDs, steroid injections, and hyaluronic acid provide temporary relief but do nothing to address the underlying bone and cartilage damage.
Bone-on-Bone Doesn't Mean Surgery Is Inevitable
Even advanced osteoarthritis with subchondral bone lesions can be treated with targeted stem cell therapy — regenerating the damaged tissue from within.
How Stem Cell Injection Works in One Day
No general anaesthesia. No hospitalisation. Your own cells harvested, concentrated, and precisely injected — all in a single session.
Bone Marrow & Adipose Harvest

A small sample of bone marrow is withdrawn from your iliac crest (pelvis) under local anaesthesia. Takes 20–30 minutes. Minimal discomfort. Adipose tissue (fat) may also be harvested for additional stem cells.
Concentration & Activation
Your bone marrow is spun in a centrifuge to concentrate mesenchymal stem cells and growth factors. Adipocyte-derived stem cells may also be harvested from fat tissue.
Targeted Intraosseous Injection
Using fluoroscopy guidance, stem cells are injected into the subchondral bone beneath cartilage damage — not just into the joint fluid. This is the Hernigou technique.
Home the Same Day
No overnight stay. Walk with assistance immediately. Begin gentle movement within days. Pain relief begins over 4–8 weeks as regeneration takes hold.
Where Are Your Stem Cells Sourced?
Stem cell treatments typically draw cells from two sources:
●Adipose Tissue (Fat): Harvested from abdominal fat, rich in growth factors
●Bone Marrow: Harvested from the iliac crest (pelvis), strongest evidence for bone regeneration
Some treatment protocols combine both sources. The prepared cell-based product is then delivered into the affected knee.

Backed by Published Science
This is not experimental. Dr. Hernigou's randomised controlled trials — published in International Orthopaedics — show consistent 15-year results across hundreds of patients.
Bone Marrow MSC Injection vs Contralateral Arthroplasty — 15-Year Follow-Up
